claims.summary: For cognition, Fisetin has moderate human evidence (28 studies).

explanation.what_it_is: Fisetin is a flavonoid—a plant compound found in strawberries, apples, onions, and other fruits and vegetables. It belongs to the polyphenol family, molecules known for their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.
explanation.how_it_works: Fisetin works primarily by neutralizing free radicals (unstable molecules that damage cells) and reducing inflammatory signaling pathways in the body. It activates cellular stress-response systems, particularly sirtuins and AMPK, which are linked to cellular repair and longevity processes. These mechanisms may help protect blood vessels, support brain function, and promote cellular resilience—though the full picture of how these lab effects translate to whole-body benefit in humans remains incomplete.

proven_benefits.note: Studies in humans show fisetin may support healthy blood pressure, endothelial function, and lipid profiles, though large randomized trials are still needed.
Human research suggests fisetin may support memory, processing speed, and overall mental clarity, though effect sizes vary and optimal dosing is not fully established.

promising_benefits.note: Animal studies show fisetin suppresses inflammatory markers, but human trials have not yet confirmed clinical benefit.
Very limited animal research suggests potential anxiolytic effects; human evidence is essentially absent.
Only rodent studies exist; no human data supports claims about muscle function or athletic performance.

explanation.emerging_research: Recent work has explored fisetin's role in cellular senescence (aging) and its potential as a senolytic—an agent that clears senescent cells. Studies in mice and cell cultures suggest promise, but human trials are in very early stages. Researchers are also investigating whether fisetin enhances the effects of other longevity-focused compounds, though these synergies remain theoretical.
explanation.caveats: Fisetin is a food-derived compound with a reasonable safety profile, but most human studies use supplemental doses higher than typical dietary intake; long-term safety at such levels is not fully characterized. Bioavailability varies widely depending on formulation, and quality/purity of commercial supplements can differ significantly—look for third-party testing.
